issues.legal_issue: An inadvertent and curable defect in the signing or authorization of an appeal does not justify dismissing it without an opportunity to rectify the defect when the appeal was filed with the appellant’s knowledge and authority.
material_facts: The organization was named as an appellant, but the appeal described it as represented by a former office-bearer and the accompanying vakalatnama was signed by an individual appellant rather than expressly by the organization.
The organization knew of the appeal, and its counsel in the trial court also filed the appeal.
The appellate court’s office accepted the appeal without raising the authorization defect, and the landlord did not object until after the individual appellant had died.
The organization’s working office-bearer applied to have the individual appellant deleted and to correct the description of the organization’s representative.
issues.conclusion: The defect did not invalidate the organization’s appeal. The appellate court should have permitted the requested correction and, at the least, given the organization an opportunity to rectify any defect before dismissing the appeal.
issues.legal_principle: Order 41 Rule 1 CPC requires an appeal memorandum to be signed by the appellant or pleader; Order 3 Rule 4 CPC governs a pleader’s authority. Under the principles in Bihar State Electricity Board v. Bhowra Kankanee Collieries Ltd., Shastri Yagnapurushdasji v. Muldas Bhundardas Vaishya, and Kodi Lal v. Ch. Ahmad Hasan, procedural defects in signing or authority may be corrected and should not defeat substantive rights where the filing was authorized and the defect is not deliberate. Such relief may be unavailable where a governing rule specifies the consequence, the defect remains uncorrected despite an opportunity, the breach is deliberate or mischievous, correction affects the merits or jurisdiction, or the appeal was presented with no authority, knowledge, or consent of the appellant.

rule.if: appeal_proceeding and representation_or_authority_defect and defect_was_inadvertent and appellant_knew_of_and_authorized_filing and defect_can_be_corrected_without_affecting_merits_or_jurisdiction and court_accepted_filing_without_raising_defect

predicates.appeal_proceeding: A party filed an appeal from a lower court’s decision.
predicates.representation_or_authority_defect: The appeal papers contained a defect concerning who represented the appellant or the authority to sign or file for the appellant.
predicates.defect_was_inadvertent: The defect resulted from an oversight or mistake rather than a deliberate or mischievous act.
predicates.appellant_knew_of_and_authorized_filing: The appellant knew of the appeal and authorized its filing.
predicates.defect_can_be_corrected_without_affectin: Correcting the defect would not alter the merits of the dispute or the court’s jurisdiction.
predicates.court_accepted_filing_without_raising_de: The court or its office accepted the appeal without raising the defect when it was filed.

issues.definition: When an authorized appellant’s appeal contains an inadvertent, correctable representation or authority defect that does not affect the merits or jurisdiction, and the court accepted it without raising the defect, the court allows correction rather than dismissing the appeal.

issues.legal_issue: A pleader’s authority given for proceedings in the trial court may extend to an appeal from those proceedings, so a separate vakalatnama need not accompany the appeal when that pleader files it.
material_facts: The organization had been represented by counsel in the trial court.
The same counsel filed the organization’s appeal from the trial court’s eviction decree.
The organization’s trial-court vakalatnama had been given to that counsel.
issues.conclusion: The organization’s vakalatnama in favour of its trial counsel was sufficient authority for that counsel to file the appeal, even without a separate vakalatnama for the appeal.
issues.legal_principle: Order 3 Rule 4(2) CPC, read with its Explanation clause (c), treats an appeal from a decree or order in the suit as a continuing proceeding for the purpose of a pleader’s appointment. Accordingly, a pleader who appeared for a party in the trial court may sign and present an appeal without filing a fresh vakalatnama; a memorandum referring to the existing authority may suffice.

predicates.appeal_proceeding: A party filed an appeal from a lower court’s decision.
predicates.party_was_represented_by_pleader_below: The party had appointed a pleader to represent it in the lower-court proceeding.
predicates.same_pleader_files_appeal_under_existing: The pleader appointed below filed the appeal under the authority already given by the party.

issues.definition: When the party’s pleader in the lower-court proceeding files an appeal under that existing authority, the existing authority suffices for filing the appeal.
